Iceland Imposes Temporary Tariffs on Logistics Equipment Imports, Rippling Through Local Transport Sector

REYKJAVIK – Icelandic logistics firms are facing mounting costs and operational delays following the government’s sudden imposition of temporary tariffs on imported transportation equipment, a measure aimed at supporting local manufacturers amid ongoing supply chain disruptions. The new tariffs, which came into effect last week, target a range of essential products including truck parts, cargo handling machinery, and storage containers.

Industry leaders say the tariffs—set at 15% on most affected goods—have already begun to impact both operational budgets and project timelines. “We are seeing immediate increases in the price of spare parts and equipment critical to maintaining our fleet,” said Ásgeir Jónsson, chief operating officer at Norðurtak Logistics. “This is putting pressure on our margins and forcing us to reconsider planned upgrades and expansions.”

The Ministry of Industries and Innovation stated the measure is a response to “unprecedented external pressures” and is intended to give domestic suppliers an opportunity to expand their production capabilities. “Our logistics sector has been heavily reliant on foreign-made equipment,” said Minister Sigríður Bjarnadóttir in a press briefing Tuesday. “This temporary policy is designed to create breathing room for Icelandic manufacturers while global markets stabilize.”

However, analysts warn that the tariffs could have immediate negative consequences for transport and logistics operators. “A significant portion of the equipment used by Icelandic firms is simply not produced domestically,” said Stefán Þórðarson, a trade policy researcher at the University of Akureyri. “The result is higher costs and potential bottlenecks, especially as firms scramble to source parts from alternative suppliers.”

According to the Icelandic Association of Transport Companies, the average cost of vehicle maintenance has risen by 12% since the tariffs were enacted, with some firms reporting delays in receiving critical shipments. “We respect the government’s goals, but the timing is difficult,” said association chair Katrín Ingólfsdóttir. “If the situation persists, we may see disruptions in delivery schedules for everything from groceries to building materials.”

The government has stated it will review the measure in three months. Meanwhile, logistics companies are bracing for continued uncertainty as they navigate the changing trade landscape.
